title: Differentiation detects morphisms of rational representations in characteristic zero
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Put $\mathfrak g=T_eG$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space, def-sc-dual-numbers]. Its canonical Lie bracket is induced by the commutator of left-invariant derivations of $F[G]$: a derivation $\delta:F[G]\to F$ at the counit $\varepsilon$ corresponds to $(1\otimes\delta)\Delta:F[G]\to F[G]$, where $\Delta$ is the comultiplication. With this bracket $\mathfrak g$ is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra]. A finite-dimensional rational representation is a vector space $M$ with a coassociative counital coaction $\alpha_M:M\to M\otimes_F F[G]$, or equivalently an action morphism $r_M:G\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$. Its differential $dr_M:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}_F(M)$, characterized by $r_M(1+\epsilon x)=1+\epsilon dr_M(x)$ on dual-number points, is linear and preserves Lie brackets. For any two such representations $M,N$ and any $F$-linear map $u:M\to N$, one has
$$\alpha_N u=(u\otimes1)\alpha_M\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\,dr_M(x)=dr_N(x)\,u\text{ for every }x\in\mathfrak g.$$
In particular, the left side means equivariance after every commutative $F$-algebra extension.

source.place: Theorem 10.23, printed pp.193-194; Proposition 10.31, printed p.196, combined with Proposition 10.15, printed pp.190-191 and Cartier Theorem 3.23, printed p.71, applied to the stabilizer of the graph of u. Also §10l, printed p.208 (full faithfulness).

proof.text: Put $A=F[G]$, with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\varepsilon$ induced by multiplication and identity. By [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra], choose finitely many algebra generators $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ of $A$. An identity tangent point is an algebra map $A\to F[t]/(t^2)$ reducing to $\varepsilon$, uniquely $a\mapsto\varepsilon(a)+t\delta(a)$. Multiplicativity is precisely $\delta(ab)=\varepsilon(a)\delta(b)+\delta(a)\varepsilon(b)$, and $F$-linearity is part of being an $F$-algebra map. The vector operations of [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] become addition and scalar multiplication of $\delta$. Such a derivation is determined on the generators by repeated Leibniz expansion, so $\mathfrak g$ embeds linearly into $F^s$ and is finite dimensional.

For a counit derivation $\delta$, set $D_\delta=(1\otimes\delta)\Delta$. The Leibniz rule follows by expanding $\Delta(ab)=\Delta(a)\Delta(b)$ and using $(1\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta=1$. Coassociativity gives $\Delta D_\delta=(1\otimes D_\delta)\Delta$, so it is left invariant, and $\varepsilon D_\delta=\delta$. Conversely, applying $1\otimes\varepsilon$ to $\Delta D=(1\otimes D)\Delta$ yields $D=(1\otimes\varepsilon D)\Delta$. Thus these are inverse linear identifications. Expanding the two Leibniz rules shows $DD'-D'D$ is a derivation; substituting the invariance identities shows $\Delta[ D,D']=(1\otimes[ D,D'])\Delta$. The invariant derivations therefore form a subspace of $\operatorname{End}_F(A)$ closed under commutator, hence a Lie algebra by [def-wf-lie-algebra]. Transport this bracket to $\mathfrak g$.

Choose a basis $m_j$ and write $\alpha_M(m_j)=\sum_i m_i\otimes b_{ij}$. The coaction axioms say $\varepsilon(b_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$ and $\Delta(b_{ij})=\sum_k b_{ik}\otimes b_{kj}$. Consequently evaluation by $g:A\to R$ gives matrices $B(g)$ with $B(gh)=B(g)B(h)$ and $B(1)=1$; evaluation by the inverse point supplies the inverse matrix. This gives the action morphism to $\operatorname{GL}(M)$; conversely the universal matrix of such a morphism gives exactly these coaction identities. This is the coaction/representation dictionary of [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary] for finite-dimensional $M$. At the tangent point $\varepsilon+t\delta$ the matrix is $1+t(\delta(b_{ij}))$. Thus $dr_M(\delta)=(\delta(b_{ij}))$ is linear and has the required characterization. Moreover $D_\delta b_{ij}=\sum_k b_{ik}\delta(b_{kj})$, so
$$\varepsilon[D_\delta,D_\eta](b_{ij})=\sum_k\bigl(\delta(b_{ik})\eta(b_{kj})-\eta(b_{ik})\delta(b_{kj})\bigr).$$
By the bracket of step 2 this is precisely $dr_M([\delta,\eta])=[dr_M(\delta),dr_M(\eta)]$. The same applies to $N$.

Let $U$ be the matrix of $u$ in the chosen bases, and write $B_M,B_N$ for the two matrices with entries in $A$. The coaction equality in the statement is exactly $B_NU-UB_M=0$. Applying any counit derivation entrywise gives $dr_N(x)U-Udr_M(x)=0$. Conversely, assume all these differential equalities. Let $I\subset A$ be the ideal generated by the entries of $B_NU-UB_M$, and put $H=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum], for every commutative $F$-algebra $R$, $H(R)$ is precisely the set of $g\in G(R)$ with $r_N(g)u_R=u_Rr_M(g)$. It is the stabilizer of the graph of $u$ in $M\oplus N$.

These $R$-points form a subgroup: the equation for $gh$ follows from $r_N(g)r_N(h)u_R=r_N(g)u_Rr_M(h)=u_Rr_M(g)r_M(h)$, and that for $g^{-1}$ follows by multiplying $r_N(g)u_R=u_Rr_M(g)$ by both inverses. The identity satisfies the equation. This holds for every $R$, so $H\hookrightarrow G$ is a closed subgroup scheme by [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. For $x\in T_eG$, evaluate its tangent point: the defining matrix becomes $t(dr_N(x)U-Udr_M(x))$, which is zero by assumption. Thus its algebra map factors through $A/I$, giving a tangent vector in $T_eH$ mapping to $x$. In particular the tangent map is surjective.

By step 1, $A/I$ is a finitely generated $F$-algebra, so $H=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)$ is an affine $F$-group scheme of finite type; its functor of points takes values in groups by step 5, as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. Since $\operatorname{char}F=0$, the first clause of [lem-sfb-affine-group-frobenius-smooth-image] shows that $H$ is smooth. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component] the identity component $H^0$ is open and closed in $H$ and, with its open-subscheme structure, a subgroup scheme; it is connected, and smooth because it is open in the smooth $H$. Being closed in $H$, which is closed in $G$, it is a smooth connected closed subgroup scheme of $G$, and the inclusion $H^0\hookrightarrow G$ factors through $H$. A tangent vector $\operatorname{Spec}F[\epsilon]\to H$ at $e$ has one-point image $\{e\}\subseteq H^0$, so it factors uniquely through $H^0$ by [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme]; hence $T_eH^0=T_eH$, and by step 5 the tangent map $T_eH^0\to T_eG$ is surjective. By [lem-sc-rational-tangent-cotangent-duality] this is surjectivity of $\operatorname{Lie}(H^0)=(\mathfrak m_e/\mathfrak m_e^2)^\vee\to\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-subgroup-tangent-generation] to the smooth connected affine finite-type $G$ over the algebraically closed $F$, the one-element family $H_1=H^0$ and $K=H$: it gives $H=G$ as closed subschemes, so the defining ideal $I$ is zero. Each entry of $B_NU-UB_M$ is then zero in $A$, proving the coaction equality and the reverse implication.

source.place: Proposition 10.15 and Corollary 10.17, printed pp.190-191; Cartier Theorem 3.23, printed p.71

proof.text: Finally, an equality $B_NU=UB_M$ in $A$ remains true after evaluation by every algebra map $A\to R$, so it gives equivariance on $G(R)$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $R$. Conversely, take $R=A$ and the universal point corresponding to $1_A:A\to A$ to recover the matrix equality itself. This proves the last sentence scheme-theoretically. Empty bases give the same equations with zero rows or columns, so the zero-dimensional representation cases are included.
